entries.name: 2/1 twill
entries.summary: A three-thread twill repeat places more warp than weft on the illustrated face.
entries.construction: Each warp goes over two picks and under one. Shifting the crossing by one yarn on successive picks produces a three-end, three-pick diagonal repeat.
entries.recognize: The visible floats are shorter than those in 3/1 twill, with a contrasting reverse.
entries.distinguish: The numbers describe warp-over and warp-under counts, not yarn colors or the number of plies.

references.title: CottonWorks: 2 x 1 Twill

entries.name: 2/2 twill
entries.summary: A balanced four-thread twill shows equal warp and weft interlacing counts.
entries.construction: Each warp floats over two picks and under two. The crossings shift by one position on each pick to form the diagonal.
entries.recognize: Both sides have the same interlacing balance, although yarn color, density and finishing may make them look different.
entries.distinguish: Balanced interlacing does not guarantee identical yarn sizes or equal thread density.

references.title: CottonWorks: 2 x 2 Twill

entries.name: 3/1 twill
entries.summary: A four-thread twill puts three warp crossings on the face for every one below.
entries.construction: Each warp passes over three successive picks and under one. The long warp floats create a face that can emphasize a colored warp over a lighter weft.
entries.recognize: Look for a strong diagonal and a face that differs markedly from the reverse when warp and weft colors contrast.
entries.distinguish: It shares a four-thread repeat with 2/2 twill but has unequal face and back interlacing counts.

references.title: CottonWorks: 3 x 1 Twill

entries.name: Arabesque
entries.summary: Interlacing curved stems and stylized plant forms create an ornamental network.
entries.construction: Textile examples combine tendrils, leaves and palmettes in repeated arrangements. The Met records printed cotton examples that echo the ornament of woven luxury textiles.
entries.recognize: Follow the connected curving stems through the repeat.
entries.distinguish: Arabesque is an ornamental vocabulary rather than one exact repeat or weave. Use a specific object’s record for its cultural attribution.

references.title: The Met: Textile with arabesque and palmette design

entries.name: Argyle
entries.summary: Colored diamonds combine with crossing diagonal lines to make a layered geometric repeat.
entries.construction: The motif is strongly associated with knitted garments. Its colored diamonds and fine overlaid lines can also be reproduced by other textile methods.
entries.recognize: Look for the thin diagonal lattice crossing through the solid diamonds.
entries.distinguish: Harlequin is usually a field of contrasting diamonds without argyle’s characteristic crossing lines. Argyle is a design, not a single knitting stitch.

references.title: Pringle of Scotland: Brand history and argyle

entries.name: Awning stripe
entries.summary: Broad, regular bands create a bold alternating stripe.
entries.construction: Wide areas of contrasting color repeat across the surface. The design appears in both shirting and furnishing textiles.
entries.recognize: Look for bands wide enough to remain distinct from a distance.
entries.distinguish: The name describes the scale of the pattern. It does not mean a dress fabric has the weather resistance or strength needed for an actual awning.

references.title: Thomas Pink: Stripe types and Bengal stripe proportions

entries.name: Basket weave
entries.summary: Groups of yarns act together to make a larger version of plain weave.
entries.construction: Two or more neighboring warps pass together over and under groups of wefts. The example is a balanced 2 by 2 basket; unequal groupings are also possible.
entries.recognize: Look for small woven blocks, with neighboring yarns following the same path.
entries.distinguish: The grouped crossings separate basket weave from a single-thread plain weave; Oxford is a familiar uneven variation.

references.title: CottonWorks: Basket weave

entries.name: Batik
entries.summary: Wax protects selected cloth areas from dye to create a patterned textile.
entries.construction: Artisans apply the wax design, dye the cloth and remove the resist. Repeated stages allow additional colors and detail.
entries.recognize: Look for reserved lines and areas, sometimes with fine dye veins where wax cracked.
entries.distinguish: Batik is a process with important cultural traditions, especially in Indonesia, not one flower or geometric motif. A batik-style print need not use wax resist.

references.title: UNESCO: Indonesian batik techniques and cultural context

entries.name: Bengal stripe
entries.summary: Alternating light and colored stripes of approximately equal width.
entries.construction: In woven shirting, repeated warp color bands create the design. Thomas Pink describes its Bengal stripe as quarter-inch alternations, an example rather than a universal rule.
entries.recognize: The light and dark bands have similar visual weight.
entries.distinguish: Bengal is generally bolder than fine shirting stripes and narrower than an awning stripe, but names and widths vary across manufacturers.

references.title: Thomas Pink: Stripe types and Bengal stripe proportions

entries.name: Birdseye weave
entries.summary: Small repeated eye-like figures give several woven constructions their birdseye name.
entries.construction: Interlacing and sometimes contrasting yarn colors outline tiny spots or lozenges. The name covers related visual effects rather than one universally fixed draft.
entries.recognize: Look for regularly spaced small eyes or dots, often clearer close up than at a distance.
entries.distinguish: A birdseye effect can arise from structure or color-and-weave interaction; it is not automatically a printed polka dot.

references.title: KSRCT: Fabric Structure and Design, birdseye and spot effects
University of Illinois Extension: textile identification, birdseye weave

entries.name: Bobbin lace
entries.summary: Bobbin lace creates openwork by crossing and twisting multiple threads.
entries.construction: Threads wound on bobbins are worked around a pattern. Pins on a supporting pillow hold the developing network in place.
entries.recognize: Close inspection reveals interlaced thread paths forming the solid and open areas.
entries.distinguish: Needle lace builds its structure with a needle and thread; many machine laces imitate either appearance.

references.title: The Lace Guild: Origins and History
The Met: Textile Production in Europe, Lace

entries.name: Botanical
entries.summary: Plants, leaves, branches and other botanical forms provide the subject of a repeat.
entries.construction: Designs may closely study specimens or stylize their outlines. Printed fabric can imitate drawn or woven effects without sharing those manufacturing methods.
entries.recognize: Look for leaf shapes, branching stems, fruit or identifiable plant forms.
entries.distinguish: Botanical overlaps floral but can emphasize foliage without blossoms. The depicted plant does not identify the textile fiber.

references.title: Liberty: Botanical Atlas design sources
Liberty Fabrics: Tapestry Leaves printed cotton

entries.name: Bouclé texture
entries.summary: Bouclé texture comes from a fancy yarn with loops or curls along its length.
entries.construction: An effect yarn is fed differently from the supporting yarns during twisting. Its extra length produces the irregular looped texture before the yarn becomes cloth.
entries.recognize: Look for curled yarn projections rather than a uniform cut pile.
entries.distinguish: Bouclé is a yarn effect used in both woven and knitted fabrics, not one weave or finishing operation.

references.title: CottonWorks: Bouclé

entries.name: Breton stripe
entries.summary: Horizontal stripes associated with the French marinière and nautical knitwear.
entries.construction: Classic marinières use contrasting stripes knitted into the garment cloth. Modern versions vary the palette, spacing and position of the bands.
entries.recognize: Look for horizontal color bands, often with a larger unstriped area near the neckline.
entries.distinguish: Historic uniform proportions describe a particular garment standard, not every contemporary Breton top. Horizontal stripes are a pattern choice, not a weave.

references.title: Saint James: La marinière, histoire d’une légende
Saint James: Breton shirts and knitwear history

entries.name: Brocade
entries.summary: Additional pattern yarns create figured decoration over a woven ground.
entries.construction: Supplementary yarns form decorative areas while the underlying fabric supplies its ground structure. These patterning yarns can differ in color or material, including metallic threads.
entries.recognize: Look for figured areas that appear raised or distinct from the background and inspect the extra yarns on the reverse.
entries.distinguish: Brocade is a woven fabric family, not simply any floral pattern or any fabric made on a Jacquard loom.

references.title: Museum of Fine Arts CAMEO: Brocade
MFA CAMEO: Silk textile with supplementary brocade weft

entries.name: Broken twill
entries.summary: A family of twills interrupts the continuous diagonal through a change in sequence or direction.
entries.construction: Warp or weft ordering is altered so that the twill line no longer runs uninterrupted. Herringbone is a recognizable example; other broken repeats need not form the same wide zigzag.
entries.recognize: Look for interrupted, reversed or staggered diagonal segments.
entries.distinguish: Broken twill is a broader construction description than herringbone, so the name does not specify one universal draft.

references.title: CottonWorks: Broken twill

entries.name: Brushed surface
entries.summary: Brushing raises surface fibers to change a fabric's appearance and feel.
entries.construction: A formed fabric undergoes mechanical surface treatment. The raised fibers can soften the outline of the original weave or knit.
entries.recognize: Look for a light fibrous halo above the underlying structure.
entries.distinguish: Brushing does not specify a fiber or weave. Technical finishing terminology distinguishes brushing from napping and abrasive sueding.

references.title: CottonWorks: Brushing
CottonWorks: Surface Finishing

entries.name: Buffalo check
entries.summary: A bold, large check commonly associated with alternating red and black blocks.
entries.construction: Matching bands cross in both directions to make the check. Woolrich’s familiar version uses wool flannel, while the design now appears in many materials and colorways.
entries.recognize: Read the big blocks first, then the mixed-color areas where the bands overlap.
entries.distinguish: The check does not make a fabric flannel: flannel refers to the cloth and its finish. Red and black is characteristic, but not the only color combination.

references.title: Woolrich: The birth of Buffalo Check

entries.name: Burnout / devoré
entries.summary: Burnout creates sheer patterns by selectively removing one fiber component from a fabric.
entries.construction: A chemical print acts on a susceptible component in a blend. The remaining component supports the more open areas of the design.
entries.recognize: Opaque and translucent areas form a deliberate pattern within the same cloth.
entries.distinguish: Devoré is a subtractive treatment, not a fiber, weave or ordinary color print.

references.title: CottonWorks: Burn-Out Printing

entries.name: Cable knit
entries.summary: Cable knitting crosses groups of stitches to make raised ropes, braids or traveling lines.
entries.construction: Some stitches are held in front or behind while neighboring stitches are worked. Working the held stitches afterward changes their order and creates a crossing.
entries.recognize: Follow the raised stitch columns through their repeated crossings.
entries.distinguish: An Aran-style sweater may combine cables with several other textures; cable knit does not describe the whole tradition.

references.title: Craft Yarn Council: Cable Knit Turtleneck
Craft Yarn Council: Teachers Handbook
V&A: Knitting Traditions of the British Isles and Ireland

entries.name: Camouflage
entries.summary: Contrasting patches, marks or pixels disrupt a recognizable outline.
entries.construction: Textile patterns arrange color areas at different scales. Their effect depends on the environment and viewing conditions as well as the design.
entries.recognize: Look for irregular interlocking areas or pixel groups rather than a simple regular spot repeat.
entries.distinguish: A fashion camouflage print does not establish tested concealment or suitability for a particular terrain. Digital describes one visual approach, not every camouflage.

references.title: National Army Museum: Camouflage through time transcript

entries.name: Candy stripe
entries.summary: A fine repeated stripe usually made with light and colored bands.
entries.construction: Shirting makers use the term for close stripes and multicolor variations. Yarn color placement produces woven examples; the name alone does not identify the weave.
entries.recognize: The repeated light and colored lines tend to read as an even, lively rhythm.
entries.distinguish: Candy and Bengal are overlapping trade terms with no universal size boundary. Check a swatch or stated stripe width instead of assuming one fixed dimension.

references.title: Turnbull & Asser: Multi candy stripe shirt

entries.name: Canvas
entries.summary: A firm, typically heavy plain-woven fabric emphasizes sturdy yarns and close construction.
entries.construction: The basic crossings follow plain weave. Substantial yarns and fabric density give canvas its characteristic body rather than a special diagonal or pile structure.
entries.recognize: Look for a coarse visible grid and a firm hand.
entries.distinguish: Canvas and duck overlap in trade usage; the name does not specify a waterproof coating or one fiber composition.

references.title: Cotton Incorporated: Cotton Canvas

entries.name: Chalk stripe
entries.summary: A suiting stripe with a broader, softer-edged appearance than a typical pinstripe.
entries.construction: Contrasting yarns form repeated lines through the cloth. A soft finish can make their edges resemble drawn chalk.
entries.recognize: Look for a pale line with visual width and some softness against the ground.
entries.distinguish: Names overlap between suppliers, so compare stripe width, spacing and edge definition. A chalk stripe is not proof that the fabric is flannel.

references.title: Indochino: What is a Chalk Stripe fabric?

entries.name: Chambray
entries.summary: A colored warp and a lighter filling create a softly mixed color in a plain weave.
entries.construction: The classic cotton version combines dyed warp yarns with white weft yarns. Both directions remain visible through the one-over, one-under crossings.
entries.recognize: Look for a subtle two-color grid, usually with more similar faces than a warp-faced denim.
entries.distinguish: A blue color does not make chambray denim: chambray is plain-woven, while conventional denim is twill.

references.title: Cotton Incorporated: Cotton Chambray

entries.name: Chevron
entries.summary: Continuous angled bands meet in repeated V-shaped points.
entries.construction: The visible zigzag can be printed, knitted or woven. Its geometry describes the design independently of the fabrication method.
entries.recognize: Follow an unbroken band through successive peaks and valleys.
entries.distinguish: A woven herringbone typically has a break at each twill reversal. Chevron is the broader zigzag motif and does not by itself establish that structure.

references.title: Sailrite: Glossary of fabric pattern names

entries.name: Corduroy
entries.summary: Rows of cut pile make corduroy’s lengthwise ribs, known as wales.
entries.construction: Extra filling floats are woven into the cloth and then cut. The exposed yarn ends form the soft parallel cords above the ground.
entries.recognize: Look for pile ridges separated by channels; wale count describes how many ridges occupy a given width.
entries.distinguish: The cords are cut pile, not knitted rib. Narrow and wide wales are variations within the fabric family.

references.title: CottonWorks: Corduroy
Cotton Incorporated: Cotton Corduroy

entries.name: Crepe weave
entries.summary: Irregularly arranged interlacings create a granular surface without an obvious directional line.
entries.construction: Floats and binding points are distributed to suppress the obvious grid or diagonal of basic weaves. Many different repeats can produce this effect.
entries.recognize: Look for a small-scale pebbled texture with no strong continuous rib.
entries.distinguish: Crepe fabric can also gain its texture from highly twisted yarns or finishing; a crepe appearance does not prove crepe interlacing.

references.title: CottonWorks: Crepe weave

entries.name: Crochet
entries.summary: Crochet forms fabric by drawing yarn through loops with a hook.
entries.construction: Chains establish a starting structure and stitches build into earlier stitches or spaces. Different stitch heights and placements create dense cloth or open motifs.
entries.recognize: Trace the chains and stitch posts; crochet may be worked in rows, rounds or joined motifs.
entries.distinguish: Hand crochet differs from knitting; industrial machinery also uses the term crochet for some warp-knitted structures.

references.title: Craft Yarn Council: Get Hooked
CottonWorks: Crochet in Warp Knitting

entries.name: Damask
entries.summary: Contrasting bindings create a figured woven design that reverses between the two faces.
entries.construction: Classical damask uses one warp and one weft, changing the interlacing between figure and ground. Satin-based examples use different float directions to change how light reflects.
entries.recognize: Tilt the fabric and turn it over: the figure and ground often exchange light and dark appearances.
entries.distinguish: Damask forms contrast through its binding systems; brocade commonly adds supplementary pattern yarns.

references.title: Fitzwilliam Museum: Damask terminology
Museo del Traje: Silk damask cloth

entries.name: Denim
entries.summary: A twill fabric commonly combines colored warp yarns with pale filling yarns.
entries.construction: Conventional denim is often a 3/1 warp-faced twill, placing more of the dyed warp on the face. Other weights and twill variations exist, including broken twills.
entries.recognize: Look for diagonal ribs and, in classic blue denim, a lighter reverse.
entries.distinguish: Denim identifies a fabric family. Selvedge describes an edge, and raw describes a finishing state; neither is a separate weave.

references.title: CottonWorks: Denim
CottonWorks: Textile Weaving, denim and 3/1 twill

entries.name: Diamond twill
entries.summary: Twill directions reverse along both axes to outline woven diamonds.
entries.construction: A pointed sequence across the warp is combined with a reversing sequence of picks. The resulting repeat turns the diagonal lines into lozenges rather than an uninterrupted diagonal.
entries.recognize: Trace the diagonal ribs to see whether they meet around a repeating diamond.
entries.distinguish: A diamond motif can be printed or knitted too; diamond twill specifically describes a woven interlacing.

references.title: Smithsonian: Coverlet history and construction

entries.name: Ditsy floral
entries.summary: Small, closely repeated flowers make an all-over pattern.
entries.construction: Tiny blossoms or sprigs are distributed across the ground. The effect can be produced as a print on many different cloths.
entries.recognize: Individual flowers remain small while the overall surface reads as a fine texture.
entries.distinguish: Ditsy describes small, scattered patterning and is not exclusive to flowers or any one brand. Liberty’s Small Betsy is one specific floral example.

references.title: Liberty: Small Betsy ditsy floral design

entries.name: Dobby weaving
entries.summary: A shaft-control system produces small repeating woven figures and textures.
entries.construction: A dobby selects combinations of shafts, moving the warp ends threaded through those shafts together. Many different interlacings can be woven this way, so there is no single dobby draft.
entries.recognize: Small dots, diamonds or other repeating geometry are common, but appearance alone cannot prove the loom type.
entries.distinguish: Dobby identifies pattern control and a fabric family, not a fourth basic weave alongside plain, twill and satin.

references.title: CottonWorks: Dobby fabrics
National Park Service: Weaving Patterns
CottonWorks: Dobby shedding

entries.name: Dotted Swiss
entries.summary: A light cloth decorated with small spaced dots, often visibly raised.
entries.construction: Traditional examples use fine plain-woven cotton with additional woven dots. Later versions use embroidery, flocking or printing, so inspect the reverse and the dot surface.
entries.recognize: A light ground separates small isolated spots; textured dots may stand above it.
entries.distinguish: A flat polka-dot print is not the same construction as a woven clip-spot or embroidered dotted Swiss. The name covers several manufacturing routes.

references.title: Vintage Fashion Guild: Dotted Swiss fabric examples

entries.name: Double cloth
entries.summary: Two layers are woven together and may be joined or exchanged to form a design.
entries.construction: Each layer has its own warp and weft system in a typical double-cloth construction. Layers can exchange positions at selected places, making reversible patterns or pockets between them.
entries.recognize: Examine both faces and an unfinished edge for two connected layers.
entries.distinguish: Double cloth is made during weaving; two separate fabrics glued or sewn together are not automatically double cloth.

references.title: Cooper Hewitt: Color Decoded, double-cloth construction
National Museum of Finland: The mystery of the double cloth

entries.name: Drill
entries.summary: A firm twill fabric is widely used where clothing needs substantial body.
entries.construction: Drill commonly uses a compact 2/1 twill in cotton or manufactured fibers. The illustrated repeat shows that interlacing rather than a particular yarn weight.
entries.recognize: Look for clear diagonal ribs in a sturdy cloth.
entries.distinguish: Drill is a fabric name, not a promise of a specific fiber or measured strength.

references.title: CBSE: Fabric Study, drill construction and uses

entries.name: Embossed texture
entries.summary: Embossing presses a relief pattern into an existing fabric surface.
entries.construction: Engraved rollers apply pressure and sometimes heat. How well the effect lasts depends on the fibers and the setting or finishing treatment.
entries.recognize: Raised and recessed areas repeat across an otherwise continuous base fabric.
entries.distinguish: An embossed texture can imitate a woven effect without using that weave; inspect the underlying yarn arrangement.

references.title: CottonWorks: Embossing
CottonWorks: Mechanical Finishing

entries.name: Embroidery
entries.summary: Embroidery creates decoration through stitches worked on or through a supporting material.
entries.construction: Threads may follow counted positions in the ground or move freely over a drawn design. Additional techniques attach laid threads or build raised details.
entries.recognize: Look for decorative stitches that can be distinguished from the ground fabric's own yarn structure.
entries.distinguish: This is a broad family of techniques; similar motifs can also be printed or woven.

references.title: V&A: Embroidery Styles, an Illustrated Guide

entries.name: Fair Isle knitting
entries.summary: Fair Isle is a Shetland colorwork tradition using stranded yarns and repeating knitted motifs.
entries.construction: Typically two colors are worked within each row or round. The unused yarn travels behind the stitches as short floats, while colors can change between bands.
entries.recognize: Look for repeating bands of small motifs and colored floats on the reverse.
entries.distinguish: Not every stranded multicolor knit is Fair Isle; the name also carries a specific regional design tradition.

references.title: Shetland Museum: Beginners Fair Isle Knitting
Shetland Heritage Shop: Fair Isle Knitting

entries.name: Flocked surface
entries.summary: Flocking attaches short fibers to a surface to create a soft, raised design.
entries.construction: Adhesive is applied in the desired pattern. Short cut fibers are deposited into it, then the adhesive is fixed to hold them in place.
entries.recognize: A pile-like motif sits on top of a distinct base fabric.
entries.distinguish: Flock is added to a substrate; woven or knitted pile is incorporated while the fabric is formed.

references.title: Cotton Incorporated: Printing Booklet, Flock Printing

entries.name: Floral
entries.summary: Flowers organize a design ranging from scattered sprigs to dense trailing repeats.
entries.construction: The flowers may be naturalistic or highly stylized. Printing, weaving and embroidery can each carry the motif.
entries.recognize: Look for petals, flower heads and stems, then note their spacing and direction.
entries.distinguish: Floral is a subject category rather than a fiber, finish or repeat size. A floral pattern is not automatically glazed chintz.

references.title: V&A: William Morris textiles

entries.name: Foulard motif
entries.summary: Small, orderly motifs repeat in a regular spaced layout.
entries.construction: Classic designs arrange compact geometric figures in rows or offset rows. The name also refers to a lightweight silk cloth and, in French, a scarf.
entries.recognize: Look for tiny individual shapes separated by a consistent ground.
entries.distinguish: Foulard is not one fixed symbol or one printing method. A dot repeat is only one possible member of this broader family.

references.title: Artlandia: Glossary of pattern design

entries.name: French terry
entries.summary: French terry pairs a jersey face with an unbrushed looped back.
entries.construction: A backing yarn forms floats behind the face. These remain unnapped, preserving the looped surface.
entries.recognize: Turn it over to see distinct loops rather than a fuzzy nap.
entries.distinguish: Woven toweling terry uses a different loop-forming construction.

references.title: CottonWorks: Single & Double Knits

entries.name: Gabardine
entries.summary: A closely set twill presents fine diagonal ribs and a comparatively smooth reverse.
entries.construction: Dense construction emphasizes a clear twill face, commonly with a steep diagonal. Fiber, yarn and finishing choices vary between wool, cotton and manufactured-fiber versions.
entries.recognize: Look for fine, closely spaced diagonal lines rather than a coarse denim-like surface.
entries.distinguish: The word gabardine does not guarantee rain protection; any water-resistance claim belongs to the particular finished fabric.

references.title: University of Arizona weaving archive: Focus on Fabrics, gabardine

entries.name: Garter stitch
entries.summary: Garter stitch makes a reversible knit with pronounced horizontal ridges.
entries.construction: When working flat, knitting every row forms garter stitch. The fabric alternates how the rows face the viewer, rather than presenting only knit faces on one side.
entries.recognize: Look for stacked horizontal ridges with a similar appearance on both surfaces.
entries.distinguish: Knitting every round in circular work produces stockinette, so flat-row instructions cannot be transferred unchanged.

references.title: Craft Yarn Council: How to Read a Knitting Pattern
Craft Yarn Council: Learn Knit Stitch

entries.name: Gauze
entries.summary: A lightweight open fabric family provides a sheer, airy surface.
entries.construction: Widely spaced yarns create an open cloth. The name can cover plain-woven versions and fabrics using leno crossings, so the exact construction needs inspection.
entries.recognize: Light passes readily through visible spaces between yarns.
entries.distinguish: Gauze is broader than leno. The fabric name alone does not establish medical suitability or any tested performance.

references.title: Cotton Incorporated: Cotton Gauze
Advanced Textiles Association: Leno weave

entries.name: Gingham
entries.summary: An even check formed by overlapping equal-width light and colored bands.
entries.construction: Traditional gingham is plain-woven from colored yarns with matching band widths in warp and weft. Crossings make pale, dark and mixed-color squares.
entries.recognize: The check repeats regularly in both directions, with intermediate tones at unlike-color intersections.
entries.distinguish: Gingham names both a familiar check and a cloth tradition; a printed gingham look need not be yarn-dyed. It lacks houndstooth’s pointed outline.

references.title: Museum of Fine Arts Boston CAMEO: Gingham

entries.name: Glen check
entries.summary: A compound check that combines smaller checks and striped areas into a larger repeat.
entries.construction: Traditional woven versions arrange contrasting yarn groups over a twill base. The illustration combines blocks of four-and-four and two-and-two colors in warp and weft over 2/2 twill. Houndstooth-like sections meet finer areas, sometimes beneath a colored overcheck.
entries.recognize: Look for several scales of checking within one large square.
entries.distinguish: Prince of Wales and glen check are often used interchangeably, while some sellers reserve Prince of Wales for an overchecked version. Compare the actual cloth instead of treating that naming rule as universal.

references.title: Indochino: What is Prince of Wales fabric?
Première Vision: Textile glossary, suiting motifs
Harriet C. Douglas: Twills, Tweeds and All-Wool Fabrics, glen check color order

entries.name: Greek key
entries.summary: A continuous angular line turns repeatedly at right angles.
entries.construction: The meandering line often forms a border. Textile makers can print it, weave it or embroider it onto a separate ground.
entries.recognize: Follow squared turns and repeated inward folds rather than curved loops.
entries.distinguish: Greek key identifies an ornamental line pattern. Schumacher’s embroidered border illustrates one method, not a required construction.

references.title: Schumacher: Greek Key Embroidery II fabric specification

entries.name: Gun club check
entries.summary: A multicolored small check closely related to houndstooth.
entries.construction: Classic examples combine a light ground with two or more darker yarn colors in a twill-based check. The illustration uses four light, four dark, four light and four accent yarns in both directions over 2/2 twill. Manufacturers also add larger windowpanes or vary the scale.
entries.recognize: Look for alternating colored broken checks within a regular repeat.
entries.distinguish: A large overcheck is optional, not the defining feature. The multicolor arrangement distinguishes a typical gun club from simple two-color houndstooth.

references.title: Première Vision: Textile glossary, suiting motifs
Holland & Sherry: HS2644 gun club and windowpane examples

entries.name: Harlequin
entries.summary: A repeating field of elongated diamonds arranged edge to edge.
entries.construction: Contrasting fills emphasize the diamond grid. The layout can be printed or constructed with colored textile elements.
entries.recognize: The units are tall lozenges rather than upright squares.
entries.distinguish: Argyle adds a fine crossing-line layer; a simple harlequin repeat need not include one. The motif does not specify fabric weight or weave.

references.title: Artlandia: Glossary of pattern design

entries.name: Herringbone
entries.summary: Alternating bands of opposing twill direction create a broken zigzag.
entries.construction: A group of right-slanting twills is followed by a group that slants left. This teaching repeat reverses a 2/2 twill with an offset at the meeting line rather than a continuous point.
entries.recognize: Look for narrow columns of slanting ribs that reverse direction with a visible break.
entries.distinguish: Herringbone describes this twill arrangement; houndstooth is a tooth-shaped color-and-weave pattern. A printed zigzag can imitate the look without this structure.

references.title: CottonWorks: Herringbone
CottonWorks: Textile Weaving, herringbone and chevron diagrams

entries.name: Houndstooth
entries.summary: A broken check whose pointed corners come from color order interacting with twill.
entries.construction: Classic woven houndstooth combines a 2/2 twill with four light then four dark yarns in both warp and weft. Printed versions reproduce the outline without that interlacement.
entries.recognize: Look for interlocking jagged checks rather than continuous zigzag bands.
entries.distinguish: Puppytooth is a small-scale version; herringbone describes a reversal of twill direction. A houndstooth image alone does not establish the fiber or construction.

references.title: Cally Booker: Houndstooth color-and-weave draft
Charles Tyrwhitt: Puppytooth weave
Vitale Barberis Canonico: Printed flannel in the Vintage range

entries.name: Ikat
entries.summary: A resist-dyeing method patterns yarn before it is woven into cloth.
entries.construction: Selected areas of yarn bundles resist dye, then the yarns are positioned during weaving. Warp, weft or both sets can carry the design.
entries.recognize: Slight alignment variation can give motif edges a feathered appearance.
entries.distinguish: An ikat-style print imitates the appearance without yarn-resist dyeing. The Japanese term kasuri identifies yarn-resist textiles in that tradition.

references.title: V&A: Africa fashion, ikat and printed cloth
MFA Boston: Japanese kasuri textiles in the 2015 acquisitions list

entries.name: Intarsia knitting
entries.summary: Intarsia forms separate color areas without carrying each unused yarn across the whole reverse.
entries.construction: Each color area has its own yarn supply. Neighboring areas connect where the yarns change, forming the image within the knitted fabric.
entries.recognize: Large color blocks have local joins at their boundaries rather than long backing floats.
entries.distinguish: Stranded colorwork carries unused colors behind the active stitches; intarsia treats the color areas separately.

references.title: CottonWorks: Designing Knit Textiles

entries.name: Interlock
entries.summary: Interlock is a double knit with a smooth, similar appearance on both sides.
entries.construction: Opposing needle sets work in alternating selections. Two yarn feeds complete one course of this interlocking structure.
entries.recognize: Both surfaces show fine knit columns rather than the contrasting face and back of single jersey.
entries.distinguish: Interlock is one specific double-knit construction; double knit does not always mean interlock.

references.title: CottonWorks: Interlock
CottonWorks: Digital Cotton Basics

entries.name: Jacquard knit
entries.summary: Jacquard knitting uses selected stitches and yarns to build pattern into a knit.
entries.construction: Machine needle selection controls where colors or textures appear. Single-knit and double-knit versions manage the unused yarns differently.
entries.recognize: Inspect the reverse as well as the face: the design is made in the stitches, not simply printed over them.
entries.distinguish: Jacquard is a patterning method, not one motif or fiber; knitted and woven jacquards are structurally different.

references.title: CottonWorks: Jacquard Knitting
CottonWorks: Designing Knit Textiles

entries.name: Jacquard weaving
entries.summary: Individual warp control allows elaborate woven designs with large or detailed repeats.
entries.construction: A Jacquard mechanism selects warp ends with more individual control than ordinary shaft grouping. It can combine different binding systems and colors within one design.
entries.recognize: Look for a design formed by the yarn interlacings, often visible in altered form on the reverse.
entries.distinguish: Jacquard describes a method of pattern control. Damask, brocade and other structures may be made with that method.

references.title: CottonWorks: Jacquard weaving
CottonWorks: Jacquard shedding

entries.name: Leno weave
entries.summary: Paired warp yarns cross around one another to secure an open woven structure.
entries.construction: Warp partners move across each other around the weft rather than remaining in fixed parallel columns. This crossing helps hold the open mesh together.
entries.recognize: Under magnification, follow the twisting warp pairs around the weft crossings.
entries.distinguish: A normal binary over-under grid cannot show the lateral warp crossings. The illustration is only a visual cue, not a leno draft.

references.title: Advanced Textiles Association: Leno weave

entries.name: Leopard motif
entries.summary: Irregular rosette-like spots evoke a leopard’s coat.
entries.construction: Textile designers repeat and stylize the markings in varied palettes. Printed cloth and woven textured versions can carry the same visual idea.
entries.recognize: Look for uneven clustered rings or rosettes rather than evenly spaced circles.
entries.distinguish: Leopard describes the image and does not imply animal-derived material. Cheetah-inspired motifs more often use solid spots, though commercial names can be loose.

references.title: Thibaut: African Leopard printed textile
Thibaut: Animal patterns in woven and printed fabrics

entries.name: Macramé
entries.summary: Macramé builds decorative textiles through arrangements of knots.
entries.construction: Lengths of cord or thread are knotted together. Repeated knots and deliberately open spaces form the design without a woven warp-and-weft grid.
entries.recognize: Visible knots anchor the cord network, often with loose lengths continuing as fringe.
entries.distinguish: A knotted textile can resemble open weaving or crochet, but its connections are tied knots.

references.title: Smithsonian Archives: Macramé
Cooper Hewitt: Sample Card of Macramé

entries.name: Madras check
entries.summary: A colorful checked cotton cloth tradition associated with Chennai, formerly Madras.
entries.construction: Colored yarn bands create checks with varied widths and color combinations. Patchwork madras joins pieces of checked cloth, while bleeding madras identifies a dye behavior rather than every modern example.
entries.recognize: Look for lively multicolor crossings and an airy shirting appearance; patchwork versions have actual seams.
entries.distinguish: A madras-looking print does not establish Indian manufacture or handweaving. Not every madras cloth is designed to release dye.

references.title: Orvis: The madras plaid shirt

entries.name: Matelassé
entries.summary: A sculpted woven surface creates a quilted-looking pattern.
entries.construction: Patterned weaving creates raised and recessed areas within the fabric. Contemporary matelassé bedding is commonly Jacquard-woven and may use a layered construction.
entries.recognize: Look for puffed geometric or floral relief that is woven into the cloth.
entries.distinguish: The quilted appearance does not necessarily mean that separate fabric layers have been stitched around batting.

references.title: SFERRA: Bari matelassé construction
Fitzwilliam Museum: Double weave and matelassé

entries.name: Medallion
entries.summary: A self-contained ornamental unit repeats as a rounded, oval or shaped centerpiece.
entries.construction: Designers build the unit from smaller lines, petals, dots or other elements. It may stand alone or repeat with open space around each figure.
entries.recognize: Look for an enclosed central focus inside each repeated motif.
entries.distinguish: Medallion describes the motif’s organization, not damask construction. A printed medallion can resemble one woven into the cloth.

references.title: Thibaut: Province Medallion printed fabric

entries.name: Mock leno
entries.summary: Grouped interlacings produce open areas that resemble leno without crossing warp pairs.
entries.construction: Yarn groups and floats encourage threads to gather into clusters around openings. Thread spacing and finishing matter as well as the lifting sequence.
entries.recognize: Look for a lacy grid whose warp threads remain in their original order.
entries.distinguish: Mock leno imitates an open appearance; true leno physically crosses neighboring warp yarns.

references.title: Thayercraft: Leno and mock leno, microscopic examples
MemphisWeaver: Leno vs. Mock Leno, maker demonstration

entries.name: Moiré finish
entries.summary: Moiré describes a rippling, watered appearance on a fabric surface.
entries.construction: A traditional route uses pressure during calendering to alter how parts of the fabric reflect light. The finished effect lies over the underlying fabric structure.
entries.recognize: Look for irregular flowing bands of light and dark, like watermarks.
entries.distinguish: Moiré is not necessarily silk, and a printed imitation or camera interference pattern does not establish a moiré finish.

references.title: CottonWorks: Calendering
Smithsonian: Rayon Taffeta Moire

entries.name: Needle lace
entries.summary: Needle lace builds an openwork fabric using a needle and thread.
entries.construction: Stitches connect to one another and to supporting outline threads. The resulting network forms lace rather than merely decorating an intact ground cloth.
entries.recognize: Look for fine stitched mesh and denser stitched areas joined into a self-supporting design.
entries.distinguish: Needle lace, bobbin lace and knitted lace can look related while their thread structures differ.

references.title: The Lace Guild: Origins and History
The Met: Gems of European Lace

entries.name: Ogee
entries.summary: Opposing S-shaped curves meet to form an undulating pointed repeat.
entries.construction: Mirrored curves create arch-like or stretched diamond shapes. The outline can be printed or built into a textured weave.
entries.recognize: Look for a curve that bends first one way and then the other.
entries.distinguish: Ogee names the curve geometry. It may form a trellis, but many trellises use straight lines or other shapes.

references.title: Regal Fabrics: Ogee and pattern glossary
Thibaut: Chandler ogee weave in Companions

entries.name: Oxford cloth
entries.summary: A basket-weave shirting groups warp yarns together to create visible texture.
entries.construction: Typically, two warp ends work together over and under each filling yarn. The filling is often heavier than an individual warp end.
entries.recognize: Look for grouped crossings and a slightly grainy basket surface.
entries.distinguish: Oxford is a fabric construction, not a collar style. The illustrated 2 by 1 grouping is not a 2/1 twill.

references.title: CottonWorks: Oxford weave

entries.name: Paisley
entries.summary: Curved teardrop forms with bent tips build an ornamental repeat.
entries.construction: The motif appears in woven shawls, embroidery and printed textiles. Interiors may contain smaller flowers, leaves or geometric details.
entries.recognize: Look for the hooked tip rather than a simple straight-pointed droplet.
entries.distinguish: The English name reflects the Scottish manufacturing center, not a claim that the motif originated there. Kashmir and Persian textile histories are central to its development.

references.title: RISD Museum: The paisley pattern in Kashmir shawls

entries.name: Pencil stripe
entries.summary: A narrow, clearly drawn stripe that resembles a fine pencil line.
entries.construction: The line is a color repeat laid over the fabric’s underlying construction. In shirting, fine colored stripes commonly sit on a lighter ground.
entries.recognize: Look for crisp narrow lines with more ground visible between them.
entries.distinguish: Pencil stripe is a trade description, not a standardized measurement. Its boundary with pinstripe varies by maker.

references.title: Brooks Brothers: Pencil stripe dress shirts

entries.name: Percale
entries.summary: A smooth plain-woven fabric is familiar as a crisp style of sheeting.
entries.construction: Warp and weft alternate one over and one under. Yarn choice, density and finishing affect how crisp or soft the finished cloth feels.
entries.recognize: Look for a fine plain-weave grid without the long face floats of sateen.
entries.distinguish: Percale describes a fabric construction and market family, not a cotton variety or an automatic quality ranking.

references.title: CottonWorks: Percale

entries.name: Pin dot
entries.summary: Tiny repeated dots create a subtle spotted surface.
entries.construction: The dots may be woven into the ground or applied as a print. Eton’s woven pin-dot shirting is one example of the structural version.
entries.recognize: The pattern can look nearly solid at a distance and separate into points close up.
entries.distinguish: Pin dot indicates small scale rather than a standardized dot diameter. Do not infer a raised surface from the name alone.

references.title: Eton: Woven pin-dot shirt

entries.name: Pinpoint Oxford
entries.summary: A finer Oxford variation retains grouped crossings with a smoother, smaller-scale texture.
entries.construction: It uses the Oxford grouping principle with finer yarns than a coarse casual Oxford. CottonWorks distinguishes pinpoint as using warp and filling yarns of equal size.
entries.recognize: Examine the small basket-like crossings under magnification rather than expecting an obvious dot print.
entries.distinguish: Pinpoint Oxford should not be confused with an arbitrary pinpoint-sized printed dot.

references.title: CottonWorks: Oxford weave
CottonWork: Our fabric, pinpoint construction

entries.name: Pinstripe
entries.summary: Fine parallel lines repeat across a contrasting ground.
entries.construction: A narrow group of contrasting warp yarns can produce the stripes in woven suiting. The same visual layout can also be printed.
entries.recognize: The stripe is much narrower than the space between stripes.
entries.distinguish: Pinstripe describes a visible color pattern. Chalk stripes usually look wider and softer, while a twill diagonal is part of the underlying weave.

references.title: Indochino: What is a Pinstripe fabric?

entries.name: Piqué knit
entries.summary: Piqué knit combines knit and tuck stitches to produce a small cellular surface.
entries.construction: Some needles hold loops while others knit, creating the texture. Single, double and six-feed piqués use different repeats, so their faces and thicknesses vary.
entries.recognize: Look for a fine dimpled or honeycomb-like texture, familiar from polo shirts.
entries.distinguish: Knitted piqué and woven piqué share a name but use different construction methods.

references.title: CottonWorks: Piqué

entries.name: Plain weave
entries.summary: Each yarn alternates over and under its neighbors in the smallest woven repeat.
entries.construction: Every warp passes over one weft and under the next. Adjacent warps reverse that sequence, giving a repeat of two ends and two picks.
entries.recognize: Look closely for a regular one-over, one-under grid with no long floats.
entries.distinguish: Plain describes the interlacing, not a plain color: the same structure can carry checks, stripes or printed flowers.

references.title: CottonWorks: Plain weave

entries.name: Pleated texture
entries.summary: Pleating folds an existing fabric into a repeated three-dimensional shape.
entries.construction: Folds may be formed in fabric before cutting or in an already sewn garment. Industrial methods can use heat to set suitable fibers into the desired shape.
entries.recognize: Look for repeated folds that change depth or open as the cloth moves.
entries.distinguish: Pleats describe fabric shaping, not a weave; their permanence and care requirements depend on the specific product.

references.title: ISSEY MIYAKE: Pleated Product Care and Construction
National Art Center, Tokyo: Miyake Issey Exhibition

entries.name: Pointelle
entries.summary: Pointelle uses small deliberate openings to pattern a knitted surface.
entries.construction: In machine pointelle, selected stitches move to neighboring needles. Knitting resumes at the emptied positions, leaving patterned holes.
entries.recognize: Repeated eyelets interrupt the knit, often arranged into lines or small geometric figures.
entries.distinguish: These openings are created during knitting; embroidered eyelet and cutwork use a different process on a ground fabric.

references.title: STOLL: Training of Manual Flat Knitting Machine, Pointelle
STOLL: Widening by Transferring Stitches

entries.name: Polka dot
entries.summary: Regularly repeated round spots contrast with a surrounding ground.
entries.construction: Dots can be printed, woven or embroidered. Their scale, spacing and arrangement determine how dense the pattern appears.
entries.recognize: Look for clearly round, repeated units rather than irregular animal-like spots.
entries.distinguish: Polka dot identifies the shape, not a particular weave. Small pin dots and textured dotted Swiss deserve closer inspection because their construction may differ.

references.title: Brooks Brothers: Large polka dot silk tie

entries.name: Ponte di Roma
entries.summary: Ponte is a firm double knit with a subtle horizontal rib.
entries.construction: Its repeat combines interlock knitting with courses worked on each needle set separately. This produces a compact fabric with similar faces.
entries.recognize: Look for fine crosswise lines on a smooth, substantial knit.
entries.distinguish: Ponte is a knit, even when tailored like woven cloth.

references.title: CottonWorks: Single & Double Knits

entries.name: Poplin
entries.summary: A closely woven plain-weave fabric offers a smooth shirting surface, sometimes with a fine crosswise rib.
entries.construction: Single warp and weft yarns alternate in a plain weave. Relative yarn size and spacing can create a subtle rib across the cloth.
entries.recognize: Look for a fine even surface without twill diagonals or grouped basket crossings.
entries.distinguish: Broadcloth can mean poplin-like cotton shirting in some markets, but the term also has other textile meanings.

references.title: Proper Cloth: Broadcloth shirt fabrics
Mutsaers Textiles: Poplin fabric guide

entries.name: Quatrefoil
entries.summary: Four rounded lobes surround a center to make a clover-like outline.
entries.construction: The motif can repeat separately or connect into a lattice. Its outline, rather than a specific textile process, defines the design.
entries.recognize: Count four lobes around each unit; pointed additions occur in some variants.
entries.distinguish: Quatrefoil names a four-lobed figure, while trellis names a network layout. A fabric can exhibit both.

references.title: Sailrite: Glossary of fabric pattern names

entries.name: Quilting
entries.summary: Quilting joins fabric layers with lines of stitching that can also form a surface design.
entries.construction: Stitches pass through the layers, often including padding between a face and backing. Their layout controls how the layers are held and where raised areas remain.
entries.recognize: Follow the stitched channels separating the fuller areas between them.
entries.distinguish: Patchwork joins pieces into a surface; quilting joins layers, and a quilt need not contain patchwork.

references.title: V&A: An Introduction to Quilting and Patchwork

entries.name: Raschel
entries.summary: Raschel is a versatile warp-knitting family used for meshes, lace and other textured fabrics.
entries.construction: Guide bars position lengthwise yarns around needles to make interlinked loops. Machine configuration and yarn selection allow both open and denser designs.
entries.recognize: An open net or lace-like surface may be raschel, but appearance alone cannot confirm the machine type.
entries.distinguish: Raschel names a knitting family, not a single mesh pattern or all lace.

references.title: CottonWorks: Knit Machinery

entries.name: Regimental stripe
entries.summary: Diagonal bands are arranged in repeated color groups, especially on neckties.
entries.construction: A tie’s cut and construction present the stripes diagonally when worn. Color order and direction can be significant in specific institutional designs.
entries.recognize: Look for a consistent diagonal sequence rather than a woven twill rib alone.
entries.distinguish: Repp describes a ribbed fabric and regimental describes a design tradition; neither is a universal synonym for every striped tie. Commercial stripes need not indicate an affiliation.

references.title: Brooks Brothers: Regimental ties
Brooks Brothers: Reverse stripe rep ties

entries.name: Rib knit
entries.summary: Rib knit alternates face and reverse stitch columns to form expandable lengthwise ribs.
entries.construction: In 1 × 1 rib, a face column alternates with a reverse column. Other arrangements, such as 2 × 2, group the columns into wider ribs.
entries.recognize: Gently stretch across the ribs to reveal the recessed columns between them.
entries.distinguish: A woven rib is an interlacing effect; rib knitting is built from loops.

references.title: CottonWorks: 1 x 1 Rib
CottonWorks: Digital Cotton Basics
Craft Yarn Council: Certified Knitting Instructors Program

entries.name: Rib weave
entries.summary: An extended plain-weave structure emphasizes ribs in one direction.
entries.construction: Plain weave can be extended along warp or weft while retaining alternating interlacing groups. Yarn thickness and close spacing determine how strongly the ribs stand out.
entries.recognize: Look for repeated lengthwise or crosswise ridges rather than a diagonal twill line.
entries.distinguish: Woven rib is structurally different from knitted rib, and a ribbed appearance alone does not identify one exact weave.

references.title: KSRCT: Fabric Structure and Design, plain-weave derivatives

entries.name: Sateen
entries.summary: A satin-structured fabric, commonly made with cotton yarns, presents a smooth face.
entries.construction: Long floats dominate the face, with scattered binding points. The illustrated five-end weft-faced repeat is a common teaching example; trade usage of satin and sateen varies.
entries.recognize: The surface is smoother and often more lustrous than a comparable plain-weave cotton.
entries.distinguish: Sateen is not a fiber or a thread-count grade, and the name alone does not guarantee one float direction.

references.title: CottonWorks: Sateen

entries.name: Satin
entries.summary: Long floats and separated binding points produce a smooth woven face.
entries.construction: The binding points are distributed so neighboring points do not create the continuous diagonal of a simple twill. This example is a five-end warp-faced satin, with one binding point per row and column.
entries.recognize: Look for extended smooth yarn surfaces and a face that catches light differently from the back.
entries.distinguish: Satin names a weave as well as fabrics made with it; it does not by itself mean silk.

references.title: CottonWorks: 5-Harness Satin
CottonWorks: Textile Weaving, satin structures

entries.name: Seed stitch
entries.summary: Seed stitch alternates knit and purl stitches into a small, pebbled texture.
entries.construction: Knit and purl stitches alternate across a row. On subsequent rows, their placement reverses rather than stacking into rib columns.
entries.recognize: Small raised bumps are distributed across both sides without long vertical ribs.
entries.distinguish: Moss stitch terminology varies by region; inspect the written repeat rather than assuming every moss pattern equals seed stitch.

references.title: Craft Yarn Council: Certified Knitting Instructors Program
Yarnspirations: How to Seed Stitch Knitting

entries.name: Seersucker
entries.summary: Alternating puckered and smoother bands give this cloth its recognizable relief.
entries.construction: In woven seersucker, selected warp groups are supplied under different tension or feed conditions. Their unequal take-up builds the puckered surface into the cloth.
entries.recognize: Look for physical puckers that remain when the fabric lies flat, not merely printed stripes.
entries.distinguish: Seersucker is not limited to blue-and-white stripes; a solid-color version can have the same textured construction.

references.title: TEXPROCIL: Textile terminology, seersucker definition
Proper Cloth: White seersucker fabric example

entries.name: Shibori
entries.summary: Japanese shaped-resist techniques pattern cloth by controlling which areas take dye.
entries.construction: Binding, stitching, folding or clamping protects portions of the fabric. Different manipulations create dots, grids, lines or ring-like forms.
entries.recognize: Look for repeat relationships that reflect how the cloth was compressed or folded.
entries.distinguish: Shibori includes more than tie-dye, and blue-and-white color alone cannot identify it. A printed shibori effect does not establish the technique.

references.title: Museum of Fine Arts Boston: Shibori methods
The Met: Recent acquisitions, shibori kimono, page 77

entries.name: Single jersey
entries.summary: Single jersey is a plain knit with visibly different front and back surfaces.
entries.construction: One set of needles forms connected loops. The face shows the legs of the stitches; the reverse shows their rounded crowns.
entries.recognize: Look for small V shapes in vertical columns on the face and a more bumpy reverse.
entries.distinguish: Jersey names a construction, not a fiber. Interlock has a different double-knit structure and more similar surfaces.

references.title: CottonWorks: Jersey
CottonWorks: Knit Basics
Craft Yarn Council: How to Read a Knitting Pattern

entries.name: Slub texture
entries.summary: Slub texture uses thicker sections along a yarn to create an uneven surface.
entries.construction: A decorative slub yarn deliberately includes localized thick places. Their spacing and size influence the texture of the finished woven or knitted cloth.
entries.recognize: Look for short thick streaks that follow individual yarns.
entries.distinguish: An uneven appearance alone cannot establish fiber content or whether the variation was intentional.

references.title: CottonWorks: Slub Yarn

entries.name: Smocking
entries.summary: Smocking gathers cloth into small folds held and decorated by stitches.
entries.construction: A wide area of fabric is gathered into regular pleats. Stitches connect selected folds to control fullness and make a textured pattern.
entries.recognize: Look for stitch-linked pleats forming compact geometric areas beside looser cloth.
entries.distinguish: Honeycomb smocking describes one arrangement; a woven honeycomb texture does not use this gathering technique.

references.title: Textile Research Centre: Smocking

entries.name: Sueded finish
entries.summary: Sueding gives fabric a fine, suede-like surface through controlled abrasion.
entries.construction: Fabric passes against abrasive rollers, commonly covered with a sandpaper-like surface. This modifies the exposed fibers rather than making a new woven or knitted structure.
entries.recognize: Look for a short, fine surface fuzz and muted luster.
entries.distinguish: Suede-like textile finishing does not make fabric into leather; commercial peach and suede finishes vary in intensity.

references.title: CottonWorks: Sueding

entries.name: Sweatshirt fleece
entries.summary: Sweatshirt fleece has a smooth knit face and a raised, fuzzy backing.
entries.construction: Backing yarns are knitted into the cloth. Napping raises their fibers to form the soft interior.
entries.recognize: The reverse looks brushed rather than distinctly looped.
entries.distinguish: This entry describes sweatshirt construction; fleece also names other pile fabrics and raw sheep wool.

references.title: CottonWorks: Single & Double Knits

entries.name: Tapestry weaving
entries.summary: Discontinuous colored wefts build a design while covering the warp.
entries.construction: Weft yarns work back and forth within selected areas rather than necessarily spanning the full width. Packing them closely hides the warp and creates blocks of color.
entries.recognize: Look for a weft-dominated face and color areas built into the fabric itself.
entries.distinguish: Needlepoint stitches are worked into an existing ground; tapestry weaving creates the cloth as it creates the image.

references.title: V&A: What is tapestry?

entries.name: Tartan and plaid
entries.summary: Crossing bands repeat in a defined color sequence called a sett.
entries.construction: Traditional tartan repeats a threadcount in warp and weft, usually on 2/2 twill. Equal-color crossings read solid; unlike colors visually mix.
entries.recognize: Follow the sequence of stripe colors and widths through a full repeat.
entries.distinguish: Plaid often means a checked pattern in North American usage; in Highland dress it also means a length of cloth. A tartan design does not by itself prove clan association, age or registration.

references.title: Scottish Register of Tartans: Pattern, sett and threadcount guidance
Scottish Tartans Museum: What is tartan?

entries.name: Tattersall
entries.summary: A light-ground check made with alternating fine colored lines.
entries.construction: Two contrasting sets of narrow stripes cross in warp and weft. Makers produce the pattern on different grounds, including plain-woven shirting.
entries.recognize: Look for open pale squares bounded by a repeating sequence of differently colored lines.
entries.distinguish: Tattersall is more specific than a generic grid but does not require one fiber or weave. Gingham generally uses broad equal bands rather than these fine outlines.

references.title: Proper Cloth: Waverly light blue and navy tattersall
Barbour: Belleview tattersall shirt construction

entries.name: Ticking stripe
entries.summary: A repeated narrow stripe associated with traditional mattress ticking.
entries.construction: Typical versions group darker lines against a pale ground. Contemporary decorative textiles use the stripe on varied fabrics.
entries.recognize: Look for restrained parallel bands, often with finer companion lines.
entries.distinguish: A ticking-style stripe is not evidence of feather-proof construction. The visual pattern and a tightly woven mattress casing are separate properties.

references.title: Ralph Lauren: Ticking stripe and patterned textile swatches

entries.name: Tie-dye
entries.summary: Bound or gathered cloth resists dye in selected areas to create a pattern.
entries.construction: The cloth is compressed and secured before color is applied. Opening it reveals rings, stripes, radiating forms or irregular areas determined by the preparation.
entries.recognize: Look for protected pale zones and color transitions associated with folds or ties.
entries.distinguish: Tie-dye is not limited to rainbow spirals or one country. Shibori and other named traditions have specific histories that should be credited when identifiable.

references.title: V&A: Tie-dyed clothing in the Lalage Bown collection
Museum of Fine Arts Boston: Shibori methods

entries.name: Toile de Jouy
entries.summary: Detailed scenic vignettes repeat across a textile ground.
entries.construction: Historic toiles used printed scenes, often pastoral or narrative, distributed across the cloth. Contemporary designers retain that format while changing the subjects.
entries.recognize: Look for groups of people, buildings, trees or landscapes treated as little scenes.
entries.distinguish: Toile can also mean a plain cloth or a garment fitting mock-up. A modern toile-style print need not have been made in Jouy-en-Josas.

references.title: Cooper Hewitt: A new twist on toiles

entries.name: Trellis
entries.summary: A connected lattice divides the surface into repeated open cells.
entries.construction: Crossing or linked lines establish the grid. Leaves, flowers or small motifs may sit within or over that framework.
entries.recognize: Look for a continuous network with open spaces between its lines.
entries.distinguish: Trellis describes a layout rather than one cell shape. A design may be both botanical and trellis, or both ogee and trellis.

references.title: Sanderson: Trellis fabrics

entries.name: Tricot
entries.summary: Tricot is a warp-knit family often made as fine, relatively flat fabric.
entries.construction: Many lengthwise yarns are guided into interconnected loops. Tricot machines commonly produce fine structures with relatively simple patterning.
entries.recognize: Look for fine loop columns and a different reverse texture; a close inspection is more useful than stretch alone.
entries.distinguish: Warp knitting uses many lengthwise yarns; weft knitting builds courses from yarn fed across the fabric.

references.title: CottonWorks: Knit Machinery

entries.name: Twill
entries.summary: Staggered yarn floats create the diagonal lines shared by a large family of weaves.
entries.construction: Interlacing positions move along by a regular step from one pick to the next. The illustrated 2/2 repeat is one member of a family that also includes 2/1 and 3/1 twills.
entries.recognize: Trace the diagonal ribs across the surface; their slope and prominence depend on the construction.
entries.distinguish: Twill is an interlacing family. Denim and gabardine are fabrics that use it, while houndstooth adds a color arrangement.

references.title: CottonWorks: Weaving Basics

entries.name: Velvet
entries.summary: An extra warp system forms a dense pile above the woven ground.
entries.construction: Pile warp yarns rise from a ground cloth to form loops that may be cut, left intact or combined in patterns. The short upright pile gives the surface its characteristic light response.
entries.recognize: Gently change the pile direction to see the shade change; examine the backing for a woven ground.
entries.distinguish: Woven velvet uses a pile warp, while corduroy forms its characteristic pile from filling floats. A velvet-like appearance alone does not identify the fiber.

references.title: V&A: Project Interwoven, examining velvet pile structure

entries.name: Waffle weave
entries.summary: A cellular woven texture forms recessed centers bounded by raised ridges.
entries.construction: Arranged warp and weft floats draw into a three-dimensional surface when the cloth relaxes and is finished. Different repeats change the size and depth of the cells.
entries.recognize: Look for repeated square or diamond-like hollows, with raised borders you can feel.
entries.distinguish: Waffle describes a surface also found in knits; check for crossing yarns before identifying a woven waffle.

references.title: Ashford: The Wheel 35, Double Heddle Waffle Weave

entries.name: Windowpane
entries.summary: Widely spaced crossing lines frame open squares or rectangles.
entries.construction: Contrasting yarn bands can create the grid in woven cloth. A windowpane may also overlay another pattern as an overcheck.
entries.recognize: Most of each box remains open ground, unlike a solid checkerboard.
entries.distinguish: Windowpane describes the visible grid, not a weave or fiber. An overcheck is any check added over a base pattern, so the terms overlap rather than match exactly.

references.title: Indochino: What is a Windowpane fabric?
Holland & Sherry: HS2644 gun club and windowpane examples

entries.name: Woven piqué
entries.summary: Raised woven ribs or small geometric textures give piqué a patterned surface.
entries.construction: The texture is built into the cloth during weaving. Commercial examples include small birdseye-like formal shirting and more pronounced patterned constructions.
entries.recognize: Look for a stable woven ground with raised dots, cords or small geometric relief.
entries.distinguish: The piqué used for many polo shirts is knitted. Woven piqué is a separate construction family, not proof of a single repeat.

references.title: Beautiful People: Thomas Mason piqué construction and shirt details
SFERRA: Bari diamond piqué matelassé

entries.name: Woven terry
entries.summary: Uncut loops project from a woven ground to create a toweling surface.
entries.construction: A ground warp holds the cloth together while a separately fed pile warp forms loops. The loom controls yarn delivery and beat-up to build the pile.
entries.recognize: Look for intact loops on one or both faces above a woven backing.
entries.distinguish: French terry is commonly knitted; check the backing instead of using the word terry alone to identify construction.

references.title: CBSE: Fabric Study, terry-cloth construction

entries.name: Zebra motif
entries.summary: Irregular branching stripes evoke the contrasting bands on a zebra’s coat.
entries.construction: Printed and woven versions vary the band width, direction and color. Designers often stylize the marks rather than reproduce a particular animal.
entries.recognize: Look for tapered, curving bands that fork or end unevenly.
entries.distinguish: Zebra is an animal-inspired motif, not a fiber or hide claim. A simple even stripe lacks its characteristic irregular branching.
